Hiragana, Katakana and Kanji: How They Work Together

Kanjidon Team · Jan 29, 2026

Japanese normally mixes hiragana, katakana and kanji in the same sentence. They are not three competing alphabets and there is no point at which kana becomes obsolete. Learn what each system contributes, then practise them together in useful words and sentences.

Hiragana: Grammatical Shape and Flexible Spelling

Hiragana represents morae, the rhythmic sound units used in Japanese. It writes particles, inflectional endings and many words that are conventionally written in kana or whose kanji is not being used. Diacritics and small kana extend the basic table, so a simple character count does not describe the whole system.

  • は in 私は marks the topic and is pronounced わ in this particle use.
  • ました in 買いました carries part of the verb’s polite past form.
  • ありがとう is commonly written entirely in hiragana.

Katakana: Loanwords, Sound and Marked Style

Katakana represents the same moraic system with different shapes and conventions. It commonly appears in loanwords, many foreign names, mimetic words, scientific terminology and visual emphasis. It does not mean every foreign concept must be katakana or that katakana words preserve the original pronunciation exactly.

  • コンビニ, convenience store.
  • パン, bread.
  • ドキドキ, a mimetic expression for a pounding or excited heartbeat.

Kanji: Meaning-Bearing Characters Inside Words

Kanji are characters adapted into Japanese writing and commonly carry lexical information in nouns, verb stems, adjective stems and names. A character can have different readings in different words, so learn complete vocabulary such as 学生（がくせい）and 生まれる（うまれる）rather than assigning one universal sound to 生.

One Sentence, Three Systems

私はコンビニでパンを買いました。 means “I bought bread at a convenience store.” 私 and 買 are kanji; は, で and the ending いました are hiragana; コンビニ and パン are katakana. The mixture makes word boundaries, grammar and lexical meaning easier to see.

A Flexible Learning Order

  • Begin kana early and connect the symbols to audio and real words.
  • Reduce dependence on romaji as kana becomes usable, but treat transliteration as temporary support rather than a failure.
  • Add useful kanji vocabulary without waiting for flawless kana recall.
  • Read mixed sentences so the three systems develop as one writing practice.
  • Give extra attention to the script that blocks your current goal instead of following a fixed duration.

Do Not Treat Third-Party JLPT Lists as Official

The official JLPT does not publish fixed post-2010 kanji or vocabulary lists for N5 through N1. A publisher may organize characters by an estimated level, but that is a curriculum choice. Check exam readiness with official sample questions across language knowledge, reading and listening.
